newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing judge rebukes potential juror.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing judge rebukes potential juror.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Tuesday sternly rebuked a potential juror who defied his order to steer clear of news accounts of the case and excused another who he said could not be impartial.
The woman who incurred the judge's wrath admitted she had listened to television reports last week when the trial began, and as recently as Monday.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch had previously ordered prospective jurors to avoid all news reports about the trial of Timothy McVeigh who is accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
"Don't talk to anybody about this matter," he told her sternly after she was briefly questioned by prosecutors and lawyers for defendant Timothy McVeigh.
Earlier Matsch excused a potential juror from serving, saying he did not believe she could be impartial.
Another potential juror, who said he was an explosives expert and had flown planes for the U.S. government, turned the tables on prosecutors by asking details about evidence from the bomb site.
The woman who had listened to news reports said she did not want to serve on the jury, but had not tried to work out what to say to be excused.

She also said she believed McVeigh was guilty. "I guess maybe I believe in an eye for an eye," she said, adding she could not see any reason why the death penalty would not be the appropriate punishment.

William Pizzi, a University of Colorado law professor and former federal prosecutor, said it was possible the judge could hold the woman in contempt of court, impose a fine or "maybe make her spend a night or two in jail."
But he added the woman would have a right to a hearing to defend herself before the judge would find her in contempt.

Other prospective jurors said they tried their best to avoid listening to radio and television reports or reading newspaper and magazine articles about the case. One jury candidate said whenever he walked into a room and a story was on the TV about the bombing he would "either turn it off or plug my ears and hum."

The woman who was excused, a German-born naturalised U.S. citizen in her late 50s, had written in a questionnaire that she disagreed with Matsch's decision to move the trial from Oklahoma to Denver to ensure McVeigh a fair hearing.

The three-times divorced woman, who said she was physically abused by two husbands, suffered from high blood pressure and feared the stress of a high-profile trial might affect her health. She was the second person publicly and immediately excused since jury selection began last week.
One woman was dismissed last week because she had been treated for stress and feared breaking down.
An explosives expert who is also a rancher and pilot told the court he owned a gun barrel firm in Mexico and in the 1970s flew internationally for the U.S. government.
Out of the blue, the man began expounding on his unanswered questions about the bombing and said he suspected the bomb was detonated electronically.

He also said a thumbnail was normally used to strip coating off the wire used to detonate a bomb, prompting him to wonder if authorities had carried out any DNA testing on the bomb debris at the site.
"That's a question driving me nuts," he said.
"I wish I could help," Patrick Ryan, U.S. Attorney for Oklahoma City, told the man, without answering his question.
The man refused to say whether he had U.S. security clearance when he worked for the government. He also said he did not know if he had ever killed anyone.
McVeigh's attorneys did not question the man.
The identity of the potential jurors is kept secret and they sit behind a wooden panel in the courtroom.
